utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hi, Andrea, thanks for coming in.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Hi. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So I don't know how much you know already about sort of my role here and why you're even here. So I thought I'd start by telling you a little bit about myself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Basically, my job is to meet with all of the students. I meet with everybody about once or twice a semester and just talk with you a little bit about how things are going, different behaviors that you might be engaging in, and thinking about any changes you might wanna make for your life if you decide that you do. It's not my job to change you. I couldn't even if I wanted to. That's not my role at all. It's really to help you think about, you know, how things are going for you and how you might like making changes or moving forward.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Does that sound okay?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: All right. So why don't we start by you telling me a little bit about yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sure. Um, as you know, I'm Andrea, I, uh, I'm a junior I'm in the marching band. I play the tenor sax.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, neat.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm also in the-- I'm a bit of a band geek. [laughter] I play, you know, in the wind ensemble and the jazz band, things like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Wow. You really are involved in music.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, [crosstalk].

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When did you start?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, I started playing about 10 years ago, actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Wow.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I started on the violin first, and then I went on, explored a little with the piano, clarinet, finally found the tenor sax, and yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Very cool. I've always wanted to be good at music. [laughter] All right. So it sounds like you're in band and a-a few other musical ensembles, any other hobbies you have or things you like to do for fun?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, you know, just hanging out with my friends or go to the beach, things like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Just kind of everyday sort of stuff?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah [laughs].

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me a little bit about your family.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, well I have one older brother he's about eight and a half old- years older than me. My parents, and I have a dog [laughs].

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Cute. What kind of dog?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He's a Golden Retriever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, nice. Okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My big boy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: [laughs] Very fun. All right. And how are things going in school for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They're pretty good. Grades have been pretty all right. Still like 3.7 ish.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay, great, so you're doing well. What sorts of goals do you have for after college- oh, after high school?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, I'd like to, you know, I'd like to, of course, graduate high school, hopefully, go to a nice Ivy League school.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, all right.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: But I mean, that might not happen. And then I'd like to go on and become a doctor. Study psychology and then become a psychiatrist or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay, you have some pretty big dreams.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's great. That's really exciting to think about that-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -and sort of be looking forward to the future and those things. All right. Well, one thing I'm going to ask you about is, um, you know, different people have sort of different things that they really value in their life. Whether it's, you know, their cultural identity or their family or their friends or job or hobbies, things like that. So here's the little sheet that goes through just some basic values that, um, might be more or less important to certain people.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Like belonging or sense of community. Again, cultural identity or family, friendship, modesty, religion, respect, self-determination and spirituality. So, when you think about yourself, which of these are kind of most important to you in terms of your life?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, I think a sense of community and belonging.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think those two and, um, respect.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Respect, okay. Can you tell me a little bit about why you picked those three?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, I think community and belonging, I kind of related them. Um, you know how I said I was in the marching band?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I really, you know, I really enjoy being in that team setting of, you know, being with other people and all working toward- together towards that one goal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: And then in terms of respect, I-I kind of view that as one of like my major like rules. Like, I-I really do think respect is important, to respect myself and respect those around me, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I place great importance in that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay, great. So sort of being a part of a group and being a part of a team gives you a sense of, um, uh, belonging, like you said.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And sort of a-a sense of purpose in a way.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes, purpose.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And then the respect is really sort of all-encompassing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not just authority, but respecting yourself, respecting your teammates or your bandmates and other people around you. Okay, that's great.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Definitely, that's right.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: All right. Well, um, one of the things I wanted to talk to you about sort of relates to belonging and your friends. So what kinds of things do you like to do when you get together with your friends?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, sometimes we just, you know, go to the movies, go to the beach, like I had said, or sometimes we just get together at someone's house, play some good board games and hang out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, and when you're hanging out with friends, is there ever alcohol involved?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell me a little bit about how alcohol fits into sort of your social scene?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, well it's mostly just for, for parties or party settings is kind of to get things going and get everything loosened up as they say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, mm-hmm. And so when you go to parties, most of the time there's alcohol there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. And how often do you think you would say you're drinking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd say, um, on a not busy month, for instance, I'd say about like two weekends out of the month. Two or three.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. So about half the time you're drinking and half the time you're not. Can you tell me what's different about the days when you choose to drink versus not to drink?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The days that we drink are mostly, like I said, they're parties, so it's more of that whole partying and dancing and, you know, having everyone have fun. And then when we don't, it's a lot more relaxed. It's a lot more hanging out, playing board games, watching a movie it's not yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it really depends on what the activity is, whether or not alcohol is gonna be there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. And do you notice a big difference or can you tell me about the difference in your enjoyment level at say a party versus a night you're playing board games?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, I think of them as-as different, I think, you know, like in playing board games and things, it's meant to be relaxing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: So it's nice to have like that kind of breather-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -versus with a party it's a lot more energetic it's, uh, after it all, it's very draining.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: But in the moment it's quite fun to dance and have fun.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. So there's sort of pros and cons on both sides?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. What are the things that you like about drinking or like about alcohol?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, it's, you know, when we drink, we-we tend to have more fun because I guess we're not, you know, everyone's drinking together. We're a lot more loosened up and relaxed-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -and not really thinking about stresses or things like that, but it can be--When it's too much drinking, it can be- can be obviously bad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. So sort of in the-the too much drinking or-or at times, can you tell me some of the less good things or not so good things about alcohol?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, a lot of times, it'll make- it'll make people stupid. [laughs] Yeah, you know, people make dumb decisions and things like that. We-we usually try to be as safe about it

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -as possible. So we'll like sleep over at a friend's house. And so that, you know, we're not driving and it's mostly within our friend group. So we're not worried about strangers putting weird things in our drinks.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: But, um, definitely some of the ideas people can have when they're stup- when they're drunk and can be really stupid.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. So you're trying to, like you said, not engage in really dangerous activities?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're trying to stay put, you're not driving. You're trying to stay with people that you trust. Um, but yet it sounds like there's still some-some things happening from time to time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sometimes. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can you tell me a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, I, especially don't like it whenever me or one of my friends, like we drink too much and we end up like throwing up or things like that, that I don't- that's not fun.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah. Throwing up is never fun.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's not.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And how often do you think that happens?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: For me, that's happened to me once. It was the first time I ever drunk and it was- it was a lot, I didn't know what I was doing. I was mixing all kinds of weird things and just kind of taking anything everyone- anyone gave me

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -and that didn't end well.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: But after that, I haven't- but I do have friends that still do sometimes, so I'll end up like having to take care of them or something and-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It kind of puts a downer on my- on my fun.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Okay. So, on the one side, some of the fun things associated with alcohol are people are just more relaxed, sorta, um, carefree can kind of let loose a little bit more, on-on the other hand, there's a little bit more, I guess, planning involved-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -because you have to make sure that you're doing it safely or as safe as you can. And then, um, there can be some other consequences like throwing up or even if it's not you, that sometimes you're stuck your-your fun is sort of ruined when you're stuck dealing with a friend who drunk too much. Okay. And the other not so good things about the alcohol?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. People can get a little like sloppy, I guess. Like they're all loose, like with people in corners doing things that should be done in private-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -and that kind of stuff.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're kind of stuck being exposed to things you don't need to see.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Got it. Okay. Um, all right. Well, you mentioned a couple of times that you've made a few decisions to try and limit the dangerous aspect of the drinking. Why did you make those decisions?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just- I've, you know, I have an aunt who is an alcoholic. So I-I see like the issues that are involved and I've seen movies and things I know that drunk driving is an issue-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: So, I, you know, I wanna be as safe as possible in those terms and be in a setting where like we can let loose but still be safe like in someone's house or sort of my parents will tell me something. But-- So, I- like I know that there are dangers involved and I guess I wanna limit that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: And so be where I have fun.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, it sounds kinda similar to your, um, your value of respect to yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: On the one hand, you- the drinking maybe helps with the belonging community to start.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If there's too much, then it sort of—

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Then it kind of defeats the purpose? [laughs]

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Right. And then with the respect, one of the things you mentioned, is really wanting to respect yourself and not sort of cross boundaries, not sort of cross lines.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Um, how do you think that the drinking fits in with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: In terms of what? In terms of respect?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think, well in a way, I do think that drinking is probably a form of disrespect to my own body because I'm not putting things- I'm putting things in it that shouldn't be there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: And then-- But in terms of at- how it is I am respecting myself, I am- I'm respecting myself by like trying to stay in someone's house and like trying to limit my drinking so I don't get to that blackout like throwing up and everything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: And try to, you know, let loose but still be in control of my behavior so I'm not gonna go somewhere with a person I met-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -into I don't know where to, I don't know what, and-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -things like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. So you're sort of looking for that balance-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -of how much you can drink to have some of the positive benefits but not cross over.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. And what have you come up with at this point? Do you have sort of a-a limit that you stick to or are you--?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I usually-- Well, I start off like I make sure that I make my own drink so I know what's in it and how much is in it. So in that way I control how much I drink. So, I usually just, you know, get one of those cups and then make one drink. And then I'll try to make it last as long as possible. And I'll be like, "All right, this is my one drink" and I'm good in that way. I still have something in my cup so people aren't gonna be like, "Oh, here. Have some more." I'd be like, "No, I'm good. I have mine," and I'll still be, you know, having some to like let loose a little.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Okay. And do you feel that that's working pretty well for you or do you sometimes exceed that limit or-or what do you think?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: For the most part, it works pretty well because, like I said, people, you know, people come asking me, trying to pressure me, I'll be like, "No, I'm good. I have- You know, I still have something. I'll get some later." And I never end up getting anything. Oh, but sometimes they'll be like, "Hey, let's take a shot," and everyone's gathered around like the kitchen or something ready to take a shot. And then at that point, I'll be like, "Oh, well, maybe I can take one more." And that's when I start, you know, falling into-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -way too much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, uh, uh, a portion of the time it's working well for you and another portion of the time maybe you would like-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -would like to make some adjustments-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -to-to make it a little smoother. Okay. So, kind of thinking along those lines, how important is it to you make some changes or make some adjustments to your drinking to sort of fit with your values and your goals for yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, I'd like to make sure that I'd, you know, in terms of respecting myself and my body, I'd like to, you know, try to drink less.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like I-I-- You know, it is nice to let loose and have fun, but I'd also like it to be so, you know, I'm not damaging my body, you know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like my liver doesn't work by the time I'm like 22.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: And, um, you know, have my friends on board with a similar mentality so we can kind of work at it together as a group, as a- as a community.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Uh-huh. So kind of combining you alls-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -goals. Okay. So, you-you have a goal it sounds like, of actually cutting back on your drinking. How important is it to you to work on that goal and on a scale of one to ten, where one is not at all important and ten is it's the most important thing right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd say about like-like a six or a seven.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd like to work on it but, you know, if I get around to it, I get around to it. If I don't, I don't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Why do you say six or seven rather than like a four?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, because I still think it's-it's important.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I still, you know. Like I said, I don't want to hurt my body. Especially going to med school like I know how things affect your body and also affect your-your social and your school work and things like. I know that once I get to college, it's not- it's not gonna-gonna work out being, you know, drinking every weekend and then like trying to wake up early and go to school, take an exam. Like I know that's not- that's not feasible. It's not a good idea.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, looking ahead, you can't keep drinking this way and reach the goals that you have for yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Well, how confident are you that you could cut down if you wanted to-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -on that same scale from one to ten?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think if I made the decision that I was going to, for sure, then I think definitely like a 10 I know it'd be going through.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, wow. Okay. Why do you say 10?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just because I know that once I make the decision, I know I can do it. It's making the decision in the first place.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. And so you mentioned the- you know, quite a few reasons why you would like to cut down. Um, have you thought at all about how you might go about doing that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, I'm thinking of maybe like trying to convince my friends without sounding, you know, dorky or something and be like, hey, you know, let's just stay in today. Like, let's not go out or something. Or just be like, hey, I'm not like-- I'm not going to drink today. And then even if my friends do, like being okay with them, drinking around me and not doing it, and then them being okay with me drinking-- Me not drinking and them doing whatever they want.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So sort of, um, trying to plan more activities that don't involve alcohol-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -and then also trying to participate in activities without drinking yourself or maybe even drinking less than you're drinking.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Does that sound like a goal you want to work on now or?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think so. I think it's-it's very feasible. I think it's possible.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Um, so I guess we'll talk about, um, less alcohol activities. I'm just making some notes to myself and then maybe, um, reducing the amount of drinking that you're doing if alcohol is involved. Okay. Um, so that-that goal sounds feasible, you said? Would it be okay if we met in a couple of weeks to sort of see how it's going?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think so. I think that's good.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Does that sound like something you'd like to do?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I really appreciate you spending the time talking to me, you know, it sounds like you have a lot of really good goals for yourself, really ambitious goals of going to medical school and, you know, becoming a psychiatrist or, um, some-some other form of physician. Um, you're really looking forward to doing well in school so you can get there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And it sounds like you have a pretty active social life and a-a lot of friends who you feel probably would be, uh, supportive, even if you cut down on alcohol and that, you know, there's a lot of benefits you see both to your body and your health, um, your school performance, and even some of the social stuff in terms of feeling a sense of belonging without having to deal with some of the gross consequences of-of, um, drinking too much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Um, so yeah, you know, it really sounds to me like you have a good plan in place and as long as you're willing and-and interested in meeting again, I'd be very excited to be able to talk with you about how it's going.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I'd like to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: All right. Great. So I'll-I'll plan to see you then in a few more weeks.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Perfect. Nice.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.text: -for her asthma. I noticed that she's been in the emergency room five times in the last year for her asthma. What's that- what's that been like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's been- it's been really difficult. Um, I hate to see her gasping for breath. And, um, I'm really worried, you know, when she has to go. Uh, so that's been-- it's really difficult when I have to take her.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, it sounds like you'd be willing to do whatever you can to try to prevent that from happening.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. I-I also noticed that, uh, it's been about three months or so since you picked up the prescription for her chronic inhaler.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Are you having some difficulties with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, I did research on the chronic inhaler and I found out that there were steroids in it and that-that I don't want her taking steroids. I did, uh, research on some of the potential side effects and some of the health problems that can result from taking steroids and I-I just don't want her to take those at all. I don't want her exposed to them at all. And then, uh, let me just go ahead and lay this out right now. Uh, because I'm sure it'll come up, but I-I do smoke. But I make sure that I do not smoke around her so that I make sure that it does not affect her. So-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -I just want to let you know that right off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Well, it sounds like you care about Sarah a great deal. You-you don't want her, uh, using steroids. You're worried about what kind of effects those would have on her and you're- you're working hard to keep your smoking away from her so it doesn't affect her asthma.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Uh, would you mind if we talked a little bit about the chronic inhaler and the medicine that you're concerned about with, you know, the steroids because, you know, I certainly don't want her using a medicine that has steroids in it, like the ones that you're worried about for athletes. Uh, can we talk about that just a little bit?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Even though, uh, even though this medicine isn't the-the medicine that's in this is in the same broad family as the steroids you're worried about, and those are called anabolic steroids.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Which build people up and have masculinizing effects.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If-if I can draw an analogy-- Again, even though this medicine is in the same family as those big broad-broad family. If I could draw an analogy, a grape and a watermelon are in the same family of fruits, you know, and obviously, grape is much smaller than a watermelon. And if you eat one grape, you'd be fine. If you ate an entire watermelon, it can make you very sick. If we look at the grape as the medicine your daughter's taking, again, it's in the same broad family, the amount of drug that your daughter is getting is very small. Uh, and not only that it's not an anabolic steroid, even though it's in the same big family. And what this drug does is actually reduces the inflammation in your daughter's lungs. And-and it doesn't even get absorbed into the body. It only goes to her lungs. And as I said, I wouldn't want your daughter taking a medication that could have the impact of those anabolic steroids. This is really safe for your daughter to use. So what-what are your thoughts about considering having her using this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, I-I guess I didn't realize that they weren't the same thing as the anabolic steroids.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Which are the ones that cause all the problems and everything. So, um, if-if you can assure me that it's not going to have those same side effects and health problems-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, def-definitely would not. I mean, probably you saw the name corticosteroid and thought, "uh-oh."

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know. And so-- yeah, and that- and that does concern people. But I do want to reassure you that this is medication that only goes to her lungs, and won't get in her body and they're not the same kind of drugs as the ones you're worried about.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Do you mind if I talk to you a little bit about what your daughter's lungs are like when she's having these inflammations and needing to go to the emergency room?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. When-when somebody has asthma, their lungs are like hypersensitive. If I could use an analogy, again, if-if you had the skin burnt off your arm, if somebody brushed up against you before he had the skin burned off your arm, it wouldn't bother you at all. But when the skin's burned off your arm, you literally react to it. Her lungs are exquisitely sensitive. Uh, and like the skin on your arm would be if the skin got burned off. And what this drug can do? This chronic inhaler is reduce the inflammation in her lungs so that her lungs don't remain exquisitely sensitive. Because otherwise, everything in the air like dust, pollen, uh, reacts with her, uh, in ways that it would not normally affect us.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And so this chronic inhaler can really prevent that from happening. Okay? Which is why it's so important to use it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The other thing I was going to tell you is that, unfortunately, uh, even though you are smoking outside and keeping the smoke away from her, the smoke on your clothes, because her lungs are so sensitive, can also affect her lungs and cause her to have a reaction. Now, something I'd like you to think about is that, if you use the chronic inhaler every day, she may not be sensitive to the smoke on your clothes, but she still maybe because her lungs are just very different than ours. Um, honestly, I'd love to see you quit smoking for you too because, you know, as you know, it's not real good for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Uh, and it would certainly help her. Um, but what I'd like you to do is to, kind of, keep an eye on what happens when she uses the chronic inhaler. And if she's still flaring up when you're around her, if there are any, if there is smoke on your clothes because it-it can flare her up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, even when it's just on my clothes?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's that sensitive. If I realized that—

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It-it-it-- Yeah. It may not- it may not when she uses the chronic inhaler, uh, but you'll need to keep an eye on that. Obviously, it would be- what would be best if it didn't get on your clothes, or you quit smoking.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. Um, so would it help, um-- You know, the thought of quitting smoking is a pretty daunting aspect.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, I know people who've tried to quit and it's-it's just it's- it's really difficult, you know. So I know, it'd be better—

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Very hard. It's very relaxing, and-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And-and it's hard to replace it with something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, it is. Um.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, uh, any thoughts on what you may be able to do to-to help at this point, if you don't choose to quit right away?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, I was thinking, um, if since it, you know, it affects her that it's on my clothes, if I only smoked while she was at school, and then changed my clothes before she came home. Would that help?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, that-that sounds like it would be great if you were able to do that. Obviously, don't smoke in the house, you know- you know.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely. I never. Never.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Um, so yeah. If you're willing to do that, that certainly would help.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Uh, again, if you get to the point sometime down the road where you're willing to quit for both you and her, uh, we'd be glad to help you do that. Because you're right it is- it's not an easy thing to do.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [chuckles]

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's really difficult.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it sounds like right now where we are, is you're willing to-to have her use the chronic inhaler-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -to try to get the inflammation down, so she doesn't need to go to the emergency room and do whatever you can at this point to keep the smoke off your clothes. And I think you're gonna see big changes in terms of, uh, her not needing to go to the emergency room, and you probably won't need to use the rescue inhaler hardly at all.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, really?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, because you'll get that inflammation down.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, that's great-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -because that's always scary when she has to use that one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah. So we'll go ahead and get both of those prescriptions ready.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Use the chronic inhaler every day, keep the rescue inhaler around if she needs it. Uh, and let's see how that works.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That sounds good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: All right. Good.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Right. So, it doesn't get in the way of your-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -every day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Mm-mm.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Right. Oh, that's good.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, um, looking back, Mike, uh, when was it that you started thinking that when you did use alcohol, um, most in your life?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, there was really not a time that I, uh-- I don't know. I-I don't understand the question really. I mean, it-- There really wasn't-- I don't really drink on a normal basis, so, I don't know-- [crosstalk]

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, that is- that is a complete, uh-- A question that is even applicable?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's fine. Okay. Um, so, what about the, uh- the first DUI, could you tell me a little bit about that? This was your second one?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And so, that's sort of why I was asking about it earlier in your life if that was a--

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It seems like every time that I, uh, do drink more than a couple of drinks, I tend to get in trouble. And, the two times that I did, I got in trouble both times. [crosstalk]

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It was those two times. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, pretty much. I mean, it's-- It sounds strange, I know, but, uh--

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like bad luck.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Actually, that-that's followed me around pretty much my whole life, the bad luck thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: But the-the-the-the-the alcohol hasn't really at all.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: But just that bad luck?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah. Is there alcohol with the- with-- Goes hand in hand with the bad luck or just--

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sure seems like it. Yeah. It sure seems like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah. Oh, okay. So-so, what about that? The-- Is there other incidences that you could think of that seems, uh, um, alcohol was there, and then your luck just sorta took a-a turn, or it was just those two times?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, you know, I don't really, um-- I-I don't really, uh, get into a situation where I-I-I drink too much. Um, you know, again, I-I realize it's my second DUI, but,, um, uh-uh, it isn't something that, um, is like a normal everyday process for me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, you know, normally when I drink, I drink one or two drinks and then I stop. Um, so, it's not like it's, um-- You know, it's not like it's something that has become a problem in my life, you know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, good. Oh, good. And-and so, where do you usually, um, have your drinks? Is it at home or, uh, out-out for, uh- after work, social drinking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, it's normally social.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It's normally social. It would be, you know, maybe in events or something like that is normally when I would, um, maybe drink more than one or two.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess I should probably just call a taxi cab or something, you know. That way, I wouldn't have this problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Would that help?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, probably, I think that would help. I think that would be something that I should, uh- I should work on.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, it sounds like you've already been thinking about, uh, ways to-to get around safely.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, or I can just stay home probably too. If I was gonna drink, I could probably stay home, then I wouldn't get in trouble either.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You have been giving this a lot of thought.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, a little bit.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, good.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, obviously, because I just don't-- You know, I don't like getting in trouble, and I don't, uh--

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Trouble's not fun.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah. So, tell-tell me a little bit more about, um, when you fi-- If you'd find yourself, and then that-that thought comes about maybe doing something other than getting in the- in the car, does that come and go, or-or is it something that you think you-- Next time you might do?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, oh, I'll never get in the car when I'm drinking again. That-- Yeah. I-I would never do that again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: This, it-- What-what-what was different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, I don't want to lose my license, you know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't, uh, you know, I don't wanna lose my license.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Wow. You-you need your license-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -to get around. You need your license for work.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, and then I-I sell cars for a living too, so--

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -um, you know, that would be, um-- You know, I don't wanna lose my job either. You know, I think those would kind of be connected together.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: And, you know, I-- You're not gonna call my work or anything for this, are you?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No, no. That's--

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That would be entirely up to you, um, to-to have that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay. I just didn't know how that worked.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because I think if they found out, I might, you know, be in jeopardy with my job. So--

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Well, you're here. And-and-and I have you give, uh-uh, credit for that. It took a lot to come in today and, um, when, um- when somebody is actually talking safety for themselves, which I-I hear you saying, um, calling a taxi or-or staying home.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, what does staying home look like for you? Is that something that-- You know, you-you talked about drinking at an event. Would staying home be--

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, you know, the Super Bowl is coming up, and that might be an opportunity where, you know, I might-- I could see myself maybe drinking that day, you know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: So, maybe I would just, uh-- I think I'll just have people come over to my house instead of going somewhere else, you know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That would work for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so, and probably a smarter thing to do. I don't wanna go through this again, you know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Uh, so, uh, would people come and drink at your house, and then they would be fine with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, an event at your house.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There you go.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, good. That sounds good. Mike, has there even been, if any, um, a time in your life when you've thought about, um, not drinking at all?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: For my first DUI, I did, uh-- I didn't drink at all for about six months. And, um, I-I-I just didn't think that, um, I really had a problem with it, so, you know, I-I did start drinking again. But, you know, again, it wasn't uh-- You know, it was a little different last time, because I was drinking a little more last time than, you know, now. I don't really drink as-as much as I used to drink, you know, um, and, you know, after you know, I quit for six months, so I kind of knew that I didn't really have a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Right. Six months. That's a long time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What were those six months like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, I know it was kind of strange. My friends didn't really hang out with me too much. Um--

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Friends?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. You know, I, uh.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Whi-which? If you don't mind me asking, which friends were those? I don't mean to get too personal, but, the friends that normally drank with you or just your-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No, my friends.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -social circles. Okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Just my social circle, I guess, uh--

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Wha-wha-what do you think made-made them n-not hang out with you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Probably 'cause I didn't- I wasn't drinking with them, I guess. I don't really know. I mean, it seemed, uh--

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Did you ask them?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, no. I really couldn't because my girlfriend really wouldn't let me hang with them. You know? I mean, it was, uh-- She said that if I, you know, kept hanging out with them guys, that she wasn't gonna be with me anymore. And I just thought that it was better for me to, you know, calm down for a little bit and, uh, maybe things would get better with us, you know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And your girlfriend's important to you-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -and that relationship was important to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, it was until she left, you know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: At the time it was important, yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Is it-- Why'd she leave?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, she left when I started drinking again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, after the six months.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: After the six months, she, uh-- You know, it's kinda, I dunno, she just said that it wasn't gonna work out, and, uh, she decided not to continue with the relationship.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, okay. So-so, um, you started drinking again, and then she left?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, it was about the same time. I really don't know which came first. It was about the same time. Uh, we were getting in a lot of arguments. I just didn't quite feel myself. You know, I-I-I wasn't-- My friends weren't around. I, uh-- You know, I missed going out with them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You felt isolated?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It was kind of weird 'cause I felt like she was trying to control me, and, uh- and uh, you know, I, uh-- And she was telling me what to do all the time, and I just, uh, didn't feel right about the whole situation. So, it was pretty much, we both decided, you know, that it just wasn't the right thing to do, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And, so you're-you're an independent guy-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -and, no one's going to tell you what to do.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, I guess. Sure. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah. So, have, uh-- So then, you started drinking again, and that was-- If you could just kind of give me a little timeframe of how long ago that was, that-that six months of complete--

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [clear throat] Well, let's see. The first one was, uh, three years ago, and then, um, this one was a few weeks ago, so, um, it's been a few years, you know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Absolutely. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It's been a few years

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, in-in what ways has, uh, drinking, um, sort of, uh-- What is kind of the good things about drinking since those couple of- those couple of years, and then-then maybe not so good things?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't really know that I can really compare good or bad. I just, uh-- You know, I just drink to be social, you know, I don't know that it really changes anything about me. It just, uh-- You know, I just drink to be social, you know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And those friends that were not hanging around with you, did they come back?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely. Yeah. As soon as my girlfriend left, I could go out with them again, you know. [laughter]

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Did they not get along with your girlfriend?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, she didn't want me going out with them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She thought that they really--

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She was separate then from your other friends and-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -those relationships just didn't come together?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She blamed the first DUI on them. She said, you know, because I was out with them, that it was pretty much, you know, they-they made me drink too much that night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And what do you think?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think she was right on that. Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, you-you--

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, if they wouldn't have gave me those shots, you know, towards the end of the night, I would've been all right. You know, I could have drove, and I wouldn't have, uh- I wouldn't have hit that mailbox.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You would have been fine if they didn't- if they didn't give you those-those shots. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, so, the-the-the mailbox, where did that come in? That was the-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That was--

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -first DUI that got you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I was on-- It was like I was a couple of blocks away from the house and I, uh, rolled up on the neighbor's lawn and I took out their mailbox.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That must have been scary.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't really remember too much of that night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, that was blackout type?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, I don't know if I was blacked out, but I just don't remember a lot of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Right. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I wouldn't really call it a blackout. I just don't really-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -remember how that happened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm-I'm sorry. I didn't mean to assume that-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -it was blackout that-- Forgive me for that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Um, so, that it was sort of after that that the girlfriend-- Your girlfriend, I don't know, well, her name. Um, your girlfriend decided-- The mailbox and she's--

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, Mary-Mary, just [crosstalk] Well, after-after I got the-the-- After I hit the mailbox-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -um, I stopped drinking for, you know, like about six months, and, uh, you know, and we were trying to work things out, but it just didn't-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -it just didn't work.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think she became a little too possessive at that point.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah. You felt like she was the only person that, um, you had in your life, you needed your friends and--

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, I think she just wanted to control me and I was tired of being controlled.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No one likes to be controlled, uh, yeah. Yeah. Uh, and, in what ways, well, did you feel that, um, uh, at any time, did you feel controlled by your friends. You said they-they made you drink those shots. That-that sounded like maybe you felt a little controlled? But-- [crosstalk]

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No, I was-- They just-- No, they weren't- they weren't really controlling me. They just-- They shouldn't have given me the last couple shots, 'cause you, they-they knew I was pretty, you know, uh, messed up before that. So-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -you know, that when they- when they-- You know, when they gave me the last, you know, couple shots, that kind of put me over the edge.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Right, they weren't looking out for your best interest at that point.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Pretty much, pretty much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And then sent you out in your car.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean I guess it was my decision to take the, uh- you know, the other shots, but I-I just-- I don't know. I really don't really remember too much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's a hindsight again.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. You can blame hindsight a little bit. I mean, that works for me. [laughter]

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hindsight? Oh, yeah, they'll-- it'll take the- it'll take the blame. Um, so, you still-- Do you still, uh, you know, you started drinking again, and then, um, the second DUI, what-- Is it the same circle of social-social circle, same friends?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [crosstalk]

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Same type of situation. [crosstalk]

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, they've been my friends since, you know, uh, since high school.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, they're important to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yeah. And-and sometimes, um, people have friends who are friends, but then there's friends who would stay on in our lives and are constant. So, these would be your constant core--

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sure, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Have you ever had, um, uh, interest outside, um, the social drinking, the friends, um, like, what do you do when you're not with them?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, well, like I'll do stuff around the house, you know, uh, cut the grass and stop, do yard work, other than that, um, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah. And any other relationship, if you don't mind me asking-- [crosstalk]

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, no, I'm single now, so, you know, I don't really, uh-- [crosstalk]

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: How's that going?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's all right, you know, I date a little bit but, uh, you know, I just don't wanna get serious right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh what-- So, what does serious look like? Um--

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, I just don't want to date someone in a regular basis. I don't really feel like I want to be in a committed relationship.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah. That's all right, yeah. That's good. It sounds like you know yourself pretty well.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sure, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Right. So, um, now that we-we are looking at, um, your second DUI and, um-- Well, so now, Mike, if you don't mind me asking, what would you do differently, um-um, from here on now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, I think I would like really think about--

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Since the co- the court sent you and we have to sort of explore what would happen if you went out and did this again.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, I mean I-I, uh- I, uh- I wouldn't drink as much, and if I- if I did, I would call, uh, a taxi or, um, you know, get some kind of a ride home, I think, 'cause, uh, you know, I just, uh-- I-I just don't wanna get in trouble, you know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah. Is there somebody that you could call?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, I don't really think about that. I guess I would have to think about that, because if I was gonna go out and drink, I would have to think about that. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess I could call it taxi cab or something, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: They'll come.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I think that will be something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah. They'll come. As long as you got the money, they'll come and get you. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I think maybe if I take some money, I'll put it like in my wallet-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -and I'll like put it in there for emergency, and that way, I'll have money. In case I get drunk, I can just call a cab, and I'll use that money to get home.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, so, when you use your-your bar money, it would be somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What's that?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your bar money would be somewhere else, not in your wallet?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Probably in my front pocket, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There you go. Okay, yeah. So, that, y-yeah.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That makes- that makes a lot of sense. So then you'd have your money tucked away someplace different.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, if I put, uh- if I put it away, then I wouldn't spend it though, you know, [unintelligible 00:18:48] have it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There-there would be a plan that I would have to-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sounds like a good plan.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -to get home. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah. So, uh, how often do you think you'll be needing that plan in the--

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It'd probably be my wallet for a while, I would think, 'cause I-- Like I said, I don't really think I have a problem with, uh- with the drinking, you know. I just-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -think that, you know, it was an isolated incident.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: And-and I, uh-- You know, I just, uh--

utterances.speaker: therapist

utterances.text: So you've got a lot of stressors right now. You're a single mom raising a two-year-old, you're working full time, and you're going back to school. What do you think would be the most helpful for us to focus on today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, I-I told the counselor that I think childcare is probably my-my biggest issue right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell me a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Um, well, my mom normally watches my son, but lately, it's kind of becoming a problem. You know, she like will back out at the last second, and so I've had to call in at work a couple of times. I've had to miss class a few times. So i-it's just stressful worrying about, you know, whether I'll be able to do those things or not.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. So I'm hearing you say that the situation with your mom's not ideal. You actually miss class sometime and had to lose some work shifts as well, and that's problematic.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Um, outside your mom, is there anyone else that can help with childcare?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, well, I have a sister, but I don't really trust her to watch my son, and I don't really know that many people that-- the only thing I can think of, I have this one neighbor who stepped in and helped one time when my mom backed out. She-she actually has, uh, a three-year-old daughter, so you know, kind of worked out.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, I don't really know her that well, but I mean, she seems nice and I-I think she did a pretty good job that night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hmm. So what I hear you saying is this neighbor was supportive when you really needed her to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Stepped in last minute. Um, when you picked up your son, you didn't have any concerns and he seemed happy?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Let's pursue that neighbor a little bit. Um, people like that, I like to think of as natural resources, but I know for a lot of people, the major problem with, uh, childcare is affordability.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Have you given any thought to, if you'll be able to afford to pay someone on a regular basis to watch your son?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I-- you know, I mean, maybe a little bit, but I don't really make that much money to be able to afford something like daycare or, you know, like full time babysitting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, I can understand that. Um, what are some of your natural skills?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I-I like cooking. I'm-I'm actually in school for culinary arts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, I bet you're a really good cook then. Um, what would you think about a plan where you worked out an arrangement with this neighbor, where in exchange for her watching your son, you would prepare dinner for her and her, um, daughter?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Um, you know, you could maybe swap a meal for child care. What do you think of a idea like that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Hmm. That's, that's interesting. I-I never really thought of something like that, but, yeah, it might work.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, I'm glad you think so. Um, so, other than this neighbor, or is there anyone else that could help you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Hmm. No, I-- you know, there-there just aren't that many people I trust right now with my son.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay, I can respect that. You-you really have to go with kind of your gut and follow your own intuition on that. Um, what about the baby's father, is he of any help?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [chuckles] No, no, not at all. He, he really hasn't been in the picture since my son was born.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay, fine. You know what? We've got one really good lead with the neighbor. I think if you would follow up in pursuing that, you might find some relief and resolve some of your childcare issues. Um, how many days a week are you in school?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's-it's three nights right now, so I have class on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday nights.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Um, so what would it look like if you had a plan where both your neighbor and your mom were helping you out?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, well, you know, if my neighbor could even just take over one day of watching my son, I think that would help my mom quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. So what I'm hearing you say is that, if you could just reduce the amount of time that you're needing your mom, she might be more supportive, more onboard?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, I think so, yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: All right. Um, so what do you think would be your next steps in working out a plan between your neighbor and your mom?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mom, you know, just, I guess talking to my neighbor and seeing if she's even interested in this idea, and if she is, you know, telling my mom about it and, you know, hopefully, that will make her feel a little better and maybe a little bit more reliable.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Sounds like you got a good plan to follow up on there. All right. Um, now you mentioned that your son is two. When will he turn three?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Just a couple months from now. He's almost three.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in that I-- in that case, I've got another idea for you. Um, what about, um, maybe when he turns three, you could enroll him in Head Start? Are you familiar with that program?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've heard of it, but I don't know that much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Head Start is a very affordable, very high-quality preschool program. Um, it was really created for parents and families, just like yours, folks who have a lower income and fewer resources, but Head Start really prepares your child both socially and intellectually for going to school. Um, and you know, by the time he turns three, you may find that that routine is something that's better for him to get used to before he starts kindergarten. Uh, would you like some more information on local Head Start sites?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, it sounds like it would be really good for my son and, you know, it would help me out in terms of childcare for sure.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. Well, good. Um, all right. It sounds like you've got a good plan there going forward. Um, now I did see from the nurse practitioner's notes, you're also working on reducing your smoking and your drinking. How's that going?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: [chuckles] Well, you know, I-I've been working on it a couple of weeks now, and honestly, it's been a lot harder than I expected. Um, trying to break my routine in the evenings, especially has-has been hard, but, um, you know, a couple of nights I have reached my goal in terms of, you know, number of cigarettes I'm going to smoke and number of drinks. So, I mean, I've done okay some days, but others, not so much.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. So what I hear you say is that it was a bigger challenge than you expected, yeah, but you're working on it. You're-you're still committed to it. So yeah, that's really to be commended. I just want to ask you one thing though. Have you thought about secondhand smoke and the dangers of that and how that might be impacting your son?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. I definitely have, so I-I try to never smoke around him, and if I do smoke at home, I always go out to the balcony to smoke.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Oh, okay, good. You know, I can tell you really have your son's best interest at heart here. You know, just from our conversation today, I can tell you're a really good mom. Um, let's reflect back on what we've discussed here so far. Now, we've got a couple of good options between the neighbor and Head Start programs for childcare. What do you see as your next steps in getting that going?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, well, I guess just first talk to my neighbor and see if she likes this idea, and then if she does, I can talk to my mom about it. Hopefully, that kind of helps her situation out. And then, um, I'm definitely want to look into the Head Start idea because I think that would be really good.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay, okay. Good. Um, I think you've got a good plan there. Um, what would you say to us getting back together, say, in two weeks, just for us to kind of revisit and see what kind of progress you've made, you know, if you've got something worked out, great, but if you've hit a bump in the road, I tell you what, we'll put our heads together. We'll come up with another plan.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: All right. Good. Well, I want to thank you again for coming in today, Sarah. It was really nice to have met you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Thanks. All right.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're very welcome.

utterances.speaker: therapist

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, there's a lot of things that bring me here today, but the one thing that I want to focus on is the fact that I really want my son to grow up in a great environment, and just have, like, more than what I had growing up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. So, you want your son to grow up in a great environment and to have more than you had?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Is that right? so that's on your mind right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes, that's on my mind. I love my son dearly, and I don't complain about the childhood I had, I had a great childhood. I just-- I guess every parent wants the best for their kids-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -and-and I really want the best for him.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Is there anything in particular that's happening right now where this is more of a concern for you than usual?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes, um, me and his father, like, we're-- We were engaged and, um, we're just not at that connection anymore. We're focused on what we want to do in life, and that's kind of put a hassle on our relationship.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What you want to do in life? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes, I want to become a social worker. I want to help people. utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you feel that your differences in career choices is-is having an impact on your relationship with your son?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes, I feel it is, and I just-- I always really wanted like a family, like me and the dad and-and the child.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I-- That's how I feel, that I love my son dearly, but I want to provide him with that, like, we are together, we're doing it together as a team-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -because now that we're going away from each other it's made things more difficult.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. Okay, so your boyfriend?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Is he your fiance or your boyfriend?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, he was my fiance, but-

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: -we called off our engagement.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay. And he's a truck driver?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.text: Does he drive long distances-

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: -or just local?
